title: Runtime Decision Graph and Observed Behaviour Catalog
author: Marco Liu
body:
Summary:
This document codifies the runtime decision graph used by Redwood’s serving runtime and pairs every major decision node with an "observed behaviour" catalog: the visible symptoms, likely root causes, monitoring signals to consult, and actionable remediation steps. The goal is to reduce MTTR by making engineering and SRE triage deterministic, and to provide a single reference that links architecture intent to operational responses.

Audience:
- Oncall engineers and SREs
- Runtime and kernel engineers
- Performance/benchmarking teams

Intended use:
- During incidents: follow the decision graph to narrow down cause domains quickly.
- During regressions: map metric shifts to code/infra changes.
- For runbook authors: copy templates and remediation patterns into service-specific runbooks.

1) Overview of the runtime decision graph (top-level nodes)
The runtime decision graph is the canonical path an incoming request traverses while the system decides: route -> capacity -> model variant -> execution kernel -> batching strategy -> fallback/serve. Each decision node has stateful and stateless branches. High-level nodes: 

- Ingress classification: auth, tenant, model_id, request_type (chat/generation/embedding), cost_tier, priority_hint.
- Routing policy: choose region/pool based on latency policy, cost policy, and privacy constraint.
- Capacity gating: accept vs queue vs reject based on pool saturation and queue depth.
- Model selection: exact model version -> quantized variant -> CPU fallback (if allowed) -> degraded-quality small model.
- Execution mapping: single-shard, multi-shard, streaming vs non-streaming kernel selection.
- KV cache decision: cold path vs warm path (cache hit/miss) and whether to serve from prefix-cache snapshot.
- Post-execution policy: score-based quality check -> telemetry enrichment -> response streaming.

2) Decision node format (how to read the catalog entries)
For each node we provide:
- Node name
- Visible symptoms (what you will see in dashboards / logs)
- Immediate metrics to inspect (names and thresholds)
- Likely root causes (ranked)
- Quick triage checklist (1-5 prioritized checks)
- Fast mitigations (short-term)
- Durable fixes (long-term)
- Owner (team / oncall role)

3) Sample catalog entries (representative nodes)
A. Node: Capacity gating / Pool saturation
- Visible symptoms:
  - Sudden rise in request_reject_rate{pool=*} and queue_length{pool=*}
  - Latency p95/p99 increase for accepted requests when queue_length > 500
  - Autoscaler activity spiking or throttled API calls to cloud provider
- Metrics to inspect:
  - pool_cpu_utilization, pool_gpu_utilization, pool_free_memory (per node)
  - queue_length{pool}, request_reject_rate{pool}, request_enqueue_latency_ms{pool}
  - autoscaler_call_failures_total
- Likely root causes (ranked):
  1. Traffic spike or synthetic load test left running.
  2. Inefficient kernel causing slow per-request token throughput.
  3. Autoscaler misconfiguration or quota exhaustion in cloud account.
  4. Imbalanced shard placement leading to hot node(s).
- Triage checklist (quick):
  1. Check traffic origin: high-traffic tenant id, ramp policy.
  2. Inspect kernel p95 token time and GPU dispatch queues.
  3. Query cluster node metrics and recent placement changes.
  4. Validate autoscaler logs and cloud quota metrics.
- Fast mitigations:
  - Temporarily increase pool capacity if automated (scale-up).
  - Apply emergency routing rule to shift non-critical traffic to lower-cost pools.
  - Reject known low-priority tenants with 429 to protect SLO customers.
- Durable fixes:
  - Rebalance shards with numa-aware placement.
  - Tune kernel batch-slicing thresholds.
  - Harden autoscaler retry logic and add run-away detection.
- Owner: eng-platform / oncall-sre

B. Node: Kernel selection / Execution mapping error
- Visible symptoms:
  - Spike in kernel_error_count or kernel_timeouts{kernel_type=*=true}
  - Requests falling back to non-optimized kernel with higher latency.
  - Telemetry showing large variance between microbenchmark and production p50/p95.
- Metrics to inspect:
  - kernel_dispatch_latency_ms, kernel_error_count, kernel_version{node}
  - model_inference_time_per_token_ms{model_variant}
  - deployment_release_id and changed image digest in last 30 minutes
- Likely root causes:
  1. Recent kernel deploy with behavioral regression.
  2. Incompatible model variant (e.g., new operator shape) leading to kernel fallback.
  3. Driver mismatch on a subset of nodes.
- Triage checklist:
  1. Check recent release IDs; compare canary vs stable telemetry.
  2. Identify nodes with kernel_timeouts and cross-check GPU driver versions.
  3. Re-run failing requests in a dev sandbox to reproduce.
- Fast mitigations:
  - Roll back kernel image on affected nodes to last known-good.
  - Force routing to alternative model variant while root cause is investigated.
- Durable fixes:
  - Add pre-merge microbenchmarks and shape-generated unit tests.
  - Improve driver compatibility matrix and node gating.
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime / kernel team

C. Node: KV cache warm/cold path and cache skew
- Visible symptoms:
  - Sudden drop in kvcache_hit_ratio{model_id} with corresponding increase in end-to-end latency.
  - Increased memory pressure on nodes holding cache snapshots.
  - Inconsistent user-level session behavior (partial context missing).
- Metrics to inspect:
  - kvcache_hit_ratio{model_id,shard}, kvcache_load_latency_ms, session_miss_ratio
  - kvcache_eviction_rate, kvcache_snapshot_staleness
- Likely root causes:
  1. Shard eviction/rebalance after node failure causing cold paths.
  2. Mismatch between session routing and cache shard mapping (routing bug).
  3. Cache snapshot corruption during serialization.
- Triage checklist:
  1. Inspect recent node rebalancing events and eviction logs.
  2. Compare session routing table to cache shard mapping.
  3. Validate snapshot integrity hashes.
- Fast mitigations:
  - Temporarily pin session routing to the pre-eviction map for affected tenants.
  - Increase ephemeral memory on hot nodes to reduce evictions.
- Durable fixes:
  - Strengthen snapshot atomicity and integrity checks.
  - Add routing-catchup mechanism for session handoff.
- Owner: eng-serving-runtime / stateful-services team

4) Instrumentation and dashboards to make the graph actionable
Minimum dashboard set (each should have per-pool, per-model, per-tenant breakdowns):
- Ingress heatmap: requests_by_tenant, request_type, auth_fail_rate
- Routing decisions breakdown: percent_routed_by_policy, fallback_rate_by_policy
- Pool health: pool_utilization, queue_length, node_free_memory, node_gpu_temp
- Kernel health: kernel_dispatch_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), kernel_error_count
- Cache health: kvcache_hit_ratio, kvcache_eviction_rate
- SLO dashboard: per-route latency p50/p95/p99 vs SLO target; error budget burn rate

Recommended alert thresholds (starting point, adjust per pool):
- queue_length{pool} > 300 -> P1 alert (risk of cascading latency)
- request_reject_rate{pool} > 1% sustained for 5m -> P2 alert
- kvcache_hit_ratio drop > 10 percentage points in 10m -> P2 alert
- kernel_error_count increases >5x baseline over 2m -> P1 alert

5) Playbook snippets (triage workflows)
A. High-latency: follow these steps in order (15–30min TTR target)
1. Confirm client-observed latency via synthetic canaries and customer reports.
2. Query SLO dashboard for p99 and error budget burn; capture time window.
3. Use decision graph entry: check ingress classification -> routing -> capacity gating -> kernel selection.
4. For each node, open the relevant metric panels (see section 4).
5. If pool saturation: apply emergency mitigations (routing rules, scale-up).
6. If kernel regressions: revert or force alternative kernel; collect core dumps and attach to incident.
7. If kvcache cold: pin sessions and warm caches for affected tenants.
8. Post-incident: open a change with RCA link, include reproduction steps and a perf test.

B. Kernel deploy rollback procedure (fast path)
1. Identify release_id and affected nodes from kernel_error_count tag.
2. Mark nodes as unschedulable in placement service.
3. Deploy last-known-good kernel image to drained subset and run canaries.
4. If canaries pass, gradually reintroduce nodes; monitor kernel_dispatch_latency_ms p99.
5. If canaries fail, continue to roll back until stable cluster state is restored.
6. Post-mortem: full binary diff and microbenchmark suite run.

6) Benchmark & profiling guidance linked to the decision graph
- For any node suspected of being CPU/GPU-bound, run the focused microbenchmark suite with the same shapes and batch sizes observed in production. Record: per-token time, kernel occupancy, memory bandwidth.
- Maintain a small reproducible harness: a docker image that can replay a request sequence with controlled seeds and session state. Include a sample CLI:

  ./perf-replay --model rwd-llama-13b --shape 2048x1 --profile=kernel --batch=1 --kv-seed=1234

- Use the following experiment matrix for kernel regressions: operator-shapes x batch-sizes x kvcache_state (warm/cold) x quantization-level.

7) Known issues catalog (short, link to full entries)
- Node GPU driver mismatches on new instance types: symptom -> kernel_timeouts on subset of nodes. Mitigation -> gate instance types in rollout. (See known-issues/gpu-watchdog-node-hang-investigation-2026)
- Rare deadlock during multi-shard eviction under heavy tail requests: symptom -> stuck requests with no cpu/gpu activity. Mitigation -> controlled shard eviction protocol. (See runbooks/numa-aware-shard-placement-eviction-playbook-2026)

8) Suggested telemetry and log examples to capture for each incident
- Correlation keys: request_id, tenant_id, route_id, node_id, kernel_id, model_digest, release_id.
- Example log line for kernel failure:
  [2026-02-12T14:03:21Z] level=error node=node-34 kernel=optimize-v3 request_id=abc123 tenant=sales dept=adops err=KernelTimeout duration_ms=12000 release_id=2026-01-30-ker-7
- Capture GPU-level dumps when kernel_timeouts exceed 3x baseline p99.

9) Ownership and escalation matrix
- First responder: oncall-sre (pagerduty).
- Kernel regressions: escalate to kernel team lead (pager).
- Capacity/autoscaler issues: escalate to eng-platform and cloud-capacity owners.
- Long-running data/state issues (KV cache corruption): involve stateful-services and infra security as required.

10) Post-incident actions and change controls
- For any P1/P0 incident triggered by a decision-node regression, create a postmortem within 72 hours with: timeline, decision-graph path taken, mitigation steps, and benchmarks that reproduce the symptom.
- Add a perf regression test to the merge-blocking suite for any kernel or routing change that caused the incident.

Appendix A: Short checklist for oncall (copy-paste)
1) Confirm: SLO impact and customer-facing symptoms.
2) Identify: affected pools, models, and nodes.
3) Decide: route/scale/rollback (pick one canonical mitigation).
4) Execute: apply mitigation and monitor 5m rolling windows.
5) Escalate: if P1 > 15m without improvement.

Appendix B: Minimal queries (Prometheus/TSDB examples)
- p99 latency for route X last 15m: 
  max_over_time(histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{route="/v1/generate"}[5m])) by (le))[15m:1m])
- kernel error rate per node: 
  sum(rate(kernel_error_count[5m])) by (node_id)
- kvcache hit ratio: 
  sum(kvcache_hits) by (model_id) / (sum(kvcache_hits) + sum(kvcache_misses))

Appendix C: Links and references
- Runtime architecture contract: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runtime-architecture/request-multiplexing-backpressure-architecture-2026
- Kernel deployment spec: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling/preemption-aware-batch-slicing-spec-2026
- KV cache runbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/runbooks/dynamic-kvcache-resilience-and-warmup-playbook-2026

Revision history:
- 2025-09-18: created by Marco Liu (draft).
- 2025-11-02: added capacity gating procedures and alert thresholds (reviewed by Priya).
- 2026-02-14: expanded kernel rollback procedure and benchmark guidance (reviewed by Jonah).

This catalog is intended to evolve as the runtime decision graph changes; please file change requests as PRs against this document and include metric diffs and microbenchmark evidence for any recommended default threshold changes.
